newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN WAGES SHOWING NO SLOWDOWN IN Q2 - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN WAGES SHOWING NO SLOWDOWN IN Q2 - HSBC.

text.p: Australian enterprise bargaining agreements have shown no sign of the wages slowdown that appeared in second quarter data released last month, the latest HSBC Markets wages report said on Tuesday.
This meant it was likely that the trough had been seen in both inflation and interest rates, HSBC said.
HSBC forecast that the average annualised wage increase (AAWI) of federal agreements formalised in the June quarter would be around 4.7 percent, level with the March quarter.
The AAWI of all current wage agreements was expected to rise to 4.9 percent, up slightly on the March quarter's 4.8 percent.

As such, while the data was consistent with the Reserve Bank's move to cut interest rate by 0.5 percentage points to 5.0 percent on July 30, the fifth cut in a year, it was a warning against further cuts, HSBC chief economist John Edwards said.
"There is little evidence that earnings outcomes are responding to lower inflation," Edwards said in a statment.

He said it was unlikely that earnings growth was below 4.0 percent, which was markedly above the annual 3.7 percent growth rate shown in the average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) data released in July.
"Earnings are persistently growing at more than twice the level of inflation," he said, adding this meant that unless output took off, the gap would remain above productivity growth.
"This means that both inflation and interest rates have probably troughed."
The report found that the pace of private sector agreements growth had slowed in the quarter, while the pace in the public sector had quickened.

The AAWI of private sector agreements certified in the June quarter slowed to 4.5 percent from 4.8 percent in the March quarter, while the public sector AAWI rose to 4.9 percent from 4.3 percent over the same period.
HSBC said the lift in public sector wages reflected a number of large univerity agreements which gave average rises of 5.1 percent for around 31,000 employees.
For all current wage agreements, the AAWI for private sector enterprise bargains slowed to 4.4 percent from 4.9 percent in March, while public sector AAWI lifted to 4.9 percent from 4.7 percent.

The 34 major federal wage bargains covering almost 62,000 employees certified in the June quarter were estimsted by HSBC to have paid an AAWI of 4.7 percent. Major agreements cover 500 or more employees.

This was slightly below the preliminary estimate of 4.9 percent issued last month, but was still well above the estimated 4.0 percent average for the March quarter and the 4.2 percent estimate for the December 1996 quarter.

The change was due to a revision in AAWI for the David Jones Ltd agreement to 3.2 percent from 5.2 percent to be consistent with methodology used by the Department of Workplace Relations and Small Business, HSBC said.
The 22 major public sector agreements were estimated to have averaged 5.0 percent in the June quarter, dominated by the university agreements.

The 12 private sector agreements, which covered about 18,000 employees, were estimated to have paid an average increase of 3.9 percent per employee, down slightly from 4.0 percent in March, HSBC said.
